problem: Every tool you've built for the CEx team — the KYC searcher, the refund processor, the ethics email analyzer — lives inside Google Apps Script, which means Google's runtime, Google's dependency versions, and Google's quotas are decided for you. The moment CEx needs something Apps Script can't do (a heavier Python NLP model for ethics email triage, a scheduled job that needs more than 6 minutes of execution time, a tool that has to talk to an on-prem database) you hit a wall: where does that code run, and how do you make sure it runs identically on your laptop, a colleague's laptop, and whatever server eventually hosts it?

Before containers, the answer was 'it works on my machine.' A script that depends on Python 3.11, a specific pandas version, and three system libraries behaves differently on a machine with Python 3.9 and different library versions. Multiply that by every engineer, every test environment, and every production server, and you get an entire category of outages caused not by bad code but by environment drift.

Why this matters for you The instant your CEx tooling grows beyond what Apps Script can host, Docker is the mechanism that lets you package a script, its exact dependencies, and its runtime into one artifact that behaves the same everywhere — your laptop, a teammate's laptop, or a production server.
concept: Docker is a platform for building, shipping, and running applications inside containers — isolated processes that share the host operating system's kernel but carry their own filesystem, libraries, and configuration. A container is not a virtual machine: it doesn't boot a separate OS or emulate hardware.
It's a regular process on the host, walled off by kernel features (namespaces and cgroups) so it only sees its own filesystem, network stack, and process tree.

The core objects in Docker are the image (a read-only template — code plus dependencies plus a minimal OS layer, built once) and the container (a running, writable instance of that image). You build an image from a Dockerfile — a plain-text recipe of instructions — and you run one or more containers from that same image, each isolated from the others.

Term What it is Image Read-only, layered template built from a Dockerfile Container A running instance of an image, with its own writable layer Dockerfile Text file of build instructions that produces an image Registry A server that stores and distributes images (e.g.
Docker Hub, GHCR) Volume Persistent storage that survives beyond a container's lifecycle
deep: Docker's isolation is built entirely from Linux kernel primitives that existed before Docker did — Docker's contribution was making them easy to use together.
Namespaces — what a container can see
PID namespace: the container gets its own process tree, starting at PID 1, unaware of processes on the host.
NET namespace: its own network interfaces, routing table, and port space, so two containers can both bind to port 80 without conflict.
MNT namespace: its own filesystem mount points, so it can't see the host's files unless a volume is explicitly mounted in.
UTS namespace: its own hostname, independent of the host machine's.
IPC namespace: its own inter-process communication resources (shared memory, semaphores).
USER namespace: can map container root to an unprivileged host user, limiting blast radius if the container is compromised.

Cgroups — what a container can use Control groups (cgroups) cap and account for CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network bandwidth per container, so one noisy container can't starve the others on the same host. A container given a 512MB memory limit is killed by the kernel's OOM killer if it exceeds that, not gracefully — the same way any Linux process is killed on OOM.
Union filesystem — how layers work An image is a stack of read-only layers, each one the delta produced by a single Dockerfile instruction.

Docker uses a union filesystem (typically overlay2 on Linux) to present those stacked layers as a single filesystem. When a container runs, Docker adds one thin writable layer on top; everything below it is shared, read-only, and cached, which is why pulling a second image that shares base layers with one you already have is fast — only the new layers download.

# Each instruction below is a new, cached layer FROM python:3.11-slim # layer 1: base OS + Python runtime COPY requirements.txt . # layer 2: just this file RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # layer 3: installed packages COPY . . # layer 4: your application code CMD ["python", "ethics_triage.py"] Order matters: because layers are cached and reused if unchanged, putting rarely-changing instructions (installing dependencies) before frequently-changing ones (copying your source code) means a code change doesn't force a full dependency reinstall on every build.
workflow: Mapped onto how you'd actually introduce Docker into the CEx tooling ecosystem, without touching the live Apps Script app:

1. Identify a candidate: a standalone script that currently runs manually or via cron-like triggers outside Apps Script — for example, a nightly Python job that pulls agent scorecard data, runs sentiment analysis on ethics emails, and writes results back to the Sheet via the Sheets API.
2. Write a Dockerfile that starts from a minimal base image (python:3.11-slim), copies in requirements.txt, installs dependencies, copies the script, and defines the CMD that runs it.
3. Build the image locally: docker build -t ethics-triage:1.0 .
4. Run it locally with the same environment variables and service-account credentials it will use in production, mounted in as a read-only volume rather than baked into the image.
5. Push the image to a registry (Docker Hub private repo, or GitHub Container Registry) once it behaves correctly.
6. On whatever host eventually runs it (a small VM, a scheduled task runner, or later a container orchestrator), pull the image and run it — the exact same bytes that were tested locally.

The key discipline this introduces to your workflow: nothing about 'how the script runs' lives in your head or in a README anymore. It lives in the Dockerfile, versioned in Git alongside the code itself.
enterprise: In a mature enterprise, Docker sits at the boundary between 'code a developer wrote' and 'a runnable, deployable artifact.' It's the packaging format that CI/CD pipelines build, that registries store, and that orchestrators (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) schedule onto compute.

Layer Role Docker plays Dev workstation Local dev environment matches prod exactly via docker-compose CI/CD pipeline Builds and tests the image on every commit Registry Central, versioned store of every build artifact Orchestrator Schedules containers onto hosts, handles restarts and scaling Production host Runs the container; the host OS itself stays minimal and disposable For a support-org tooling stack like CEx's, Docker typically shows up first not for the whole application but for auxiliary services: a small internal API, a scheduled data-processing job, or a self-hosted monitoring agent — exactly the kind of thing Apps Script can't host.
dependencies: Docker itself depends on a working kernel-level foundation; without these, the daemon won't run or containers won't isolate properly.
Linux kernel with namespace and cgroup support (Docker Desktop on Windows/Mac runs a lightweight Linux VM to provide this).
A container runtime beneath the Docker CLI — containerd, which itself calls runc to actually create the namespaced, cgrouped process.
A storage driver (overlay2 on modern Linux) that implements the union filesystem layering described above.
Networking components (bridge networks, iptables rules) that Docker configures automatically for container-to-container and container-to-host traffic.
A registry (local or remote) to pull base images from — nothing builds without FROM resolving to something.
dependents: Once Docker is in place, an entire tier of practices and tools become possible that weren't before:
Kubernetes and every other orchestrator — they schedule containers, so without a container runtime there's nothing to schedule.
CI/CD pipelines that build a container image as the deployable artifact, ensuring what's tested is exactly what ships.
docker-compose, for wiring multiple containers (an app, a database, a cache) into one local dev environment with one command.
Immutable infrastructure practices — instead of patching a running server, you rebuild the image and redeploy.
Microservices architectures, which lean on containers to isolate each service's dependencies from the others.
security: Containers share the host kernel, which is Docker's biggest performance advantage and its biggest security caveat: a kernel-level exploit inside a container can, in principle, reach the host. Treat container isolation as strong but not equivalent to a VM's hardware-enforced boundary.

Risk Mitigation Running as root inside the container Add a USER instruction in the Dockerfile; never run app processes as root Bloated images with unnecessary tools Use minimal base images (slim, alpine, distroless);

smaller attack surface Risk Mitigation Secrets baked into image layers Never COPY secrets in; inject via environment variables or a secrets manager at runtime Outdated base images with known CVEs Pin versions, scan images (Trivy, Docker Scout), rebuild on a schedule Container escape via excessive privileges Avoid --privileged; drop Linux capabilities you don't need Unrestricted container-to-container traffic Use custom networks and explicit port exposure, not the default bridge for everything For anything touching KYC or refund data, treat a container exactly like you'd treat a production server:
least privilege, no baked-in credentials, and a documented patching cadence for the base image.

example: A support organization the size of FundedNext's typically containerizes its internal tooling in stages, not all at once. A realistic first step: the nightly job that aggregates agent scorecard metrics — currently, imagine it as a script triggered by an Apps Script time-driven trigger, limited to a 6-minute execution window and Apps Script's available libraries.

Once that job needs a heavier statistical library or a longer runtime than Apps Script allows, the natural move is to rewrite it in Python, wrap it in a Dockerfile, and run it as a scheduled container on a small VM or a managed container service — while the Apps Script front end (the part CEx agents actually interact with) stays exactly where it is and simply reads the results the container wrote back to the Sheet or a database.

Pattern to notice Enterprises rarely containerize everything at once. They containerize the piece that has outgrown its current host, while leaving stable pieces alone. That's the same incremental instinct you've already used building the Apps Script platform itself.
cloud: Every major cloud provider offers a managed way to run containers without operating the underlying VMs yourself:

Provider Service What it abstracts away Google Cloud Cloud Run Servers entirely — you give it an image, it scales 0→N on demand Google Cloud GKE (Kubernetes) Cluster orchestration, not the underlying compute AWS ECS / Fargate Server management (Fargate) or cluster ops (ECS on EC2) Azure Container Apps / AKS Same pattern — serverless containers or managed Kubernetes Given that CEx's existing stack is entirely Google-based (Sheets, Apps Script), Cloud Run is the most natural next step if a piece of tooling outgrows Apps Script: push a Docker image, and Google runs it on demand, scaling to zero when idle so you pay nothing between runs.
automation: Docker is what makes CI/CD pipelines trustworthy: the artifact tested in the pipeline is the exact artifact deployed, not a rebuild that might differ.
# Typical CI step (conceptual, e.g. GitHub Actions) - name: Build image run: docker build -t registry/ethics-triage:${{ github.sha }} .

- name: Run tests inside the container run: docker run --rm registry/ethics-triage:${{ github.sha }} pytest - name: Push if tests pass run: docker push registry/ethics-triage:${{ github.sha }} Tagging images with the Git commit SHA (rather than just 'latest') means every deployed container is traceable back to the exact code and Dockerfile that produced it — critical for debugging and for compliance in a fintech environment.
career: Docker is close to table stakes for infrastructure, DevOps, and increasingly support-engineering roles — job postings that mention 'containerization' or 'Kubernetes' assume Docker fluency as a prerequisite, not a differentiator.

For your specific trajectory — support/operations background moving toward sysadmin/infrastructure — Docker is a strong proof point precisely because it bridges the two worlds: it's the tool that lets a support engineer who can script start shipping reliable services instead of one-off scripts. Being able to say 'I containerized the internal tooling I built for my team' is a concrete, verifiable claim that a hiring manager can ask you to elaborate on in an interview.

misconceptions: Misconception Reality A container is a lightweight VM It's an isolated process sharing the host kernel — no hypervisor, no guest OS Docker makes an app secure by default Isolation reduces some risks but shared-kernel escapes are real; hardening is still required Data in a container is safe across restarts The writable layer is ephemeral by default — only volumes persist Misconception Reality Bigger base images are safer because they have more tools More installed software means more CVEs and a larger attack surface You need Kubernetes to use Docker usefully A single docker run or docker-compose file is a complete, valid deployment for many workloads
anchors: Image = recipe (read-only, layered). Container = the meal being cooked from it (running, writable).
Namespaces decide what a container can SEE. Cgroups decide what a container can USE.
A container is a process wearing a costume, not a computer inside a computer.
Layer order in a Dockerfile = 'put the stuff that changes least at the top' for cache efficiency.
docker logs = what happened. docker inspect = how it's configured. docker exec = go look inside.

lab: Hands-on: containerize a small piece of CEx-adjacent tooling — a script that reads a CSV export of ethics-flagged emails and prints a summary — to feel the full build/run/inspect cycle.
15. Create a project folder with a summarize.py that reads a CSV and prints counts by category.
17. Write a Dockerfile using python:3.11-slim as the base, copying requirements.txt first, running pip install, then copying the script.
18. Build the image: docker build -t ethics-summary:1.0 .

19. Run it, mounting a local ./data folder read-only into the container: docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/data:/data:ro" ethics-summary:1.0 20. Inspect the image layers: docker history ethics-summary:1.0 — note which instruction produced the largest layer.
21. Deliberately break the cache: touch summarize.py and rebuild, then reorder the Dockerfile so COPY . . comes after RUN pip install, and observe which layers rebuild vs. stay cached.
22. Clean up: docker system prune to reclaim disk space, and note what it removed.

Production tie-in This lab is deliberately scoped so it can become a real internal tool: swap the sample CSV for a live export path, and this is the shape of the container you'd eventually deploy on Cloud Run to offload heavier ethics-email analysis away from Apps Script's execution limits.
